newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish sects hit by anti-state, sex charges.
newsitem.headline: Turkish sects hit by anti-state, sex charges.

text.p: Turkey's secularist establishment has hit at members of a fundamentalist Islamist group with allegations of sexual misdeeds and political activities that have highlighted the country's wariness of resurgent sects.
Muslum Gunduz, leader of the Aczmendi group, faces five to ten years in prison on charges of anti-secular activities, according to a state prosecutor quoted by Anatolian news agency.

Gunduz was captured naked in the company of a 22-year-old woman, Fadime Sahin, in a raid on a house in late December by police accompanied by television camera crews. Police had been seeking him for two years under the anti-secularism charges.

"This is a plot. I am a fugitive and they must have been able to take me on my own. They came in 15 minutes after Fadime arrived," newspapers on Tuesday reported Gunduz as saying on a tape recorded in prison.
A trial begins on Wednesday of another 121 members of his Aczmendi group, facing up to five years in prison for an Islamist protest last year at Ankara's main mosque, where they clashed with police.
The Aczmendis, easily recognised by their long hair, beards and flowing dark robes, often worship in an ecstatic rite, dancing to the beat of drums.

Authorities in Moslem but secular, Turkey have long been wary of the group. The founder of modern Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, outlawed Islamic sects in the 1920s but the groups have quietly flourished again in recent years.
This week Sahin gave a statement to an Istanbul court alleging that she was pressurised into sexual relations both by Gunduz and a 'sheikh' who heads the lodge of another Islamic sect in Istanbul.

She alleged that other girls, including the daughter of a well-known Islamist MP from the ruling Welfare Party, were linked to the sheikh. The charges have sparked a furious debate by Islamists and secularists in the nation's media.
"Every day so many of our Moslem girls and women are being deceived by charlatans and not a sound comes from the poor things," said Emin Colasan, columnist for the mass-circulation daily, Hurriyet.
"Muslum Gunduz, a guru who calls himself an Aczmendi but has no connection with Islam, is just one of them," he said.
Sahin, dressed in traditional Islamic fashion with a headscarf and long coat, has been promoted by her lawyer as a symbol of women repressed by religious fanatics.
She took part in rowdy television debate on Monday night alongside the 'sheikh', Ali Kalkanci, who was later taken away by anti-terror police although the charge against him was not known.
